newsitem.title: USA: SEC asks stock exchanges to improve linking system.
newsitem.headline: SEC asks stock exchanges to improve linking system.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission has requested that the nation's stock exchanges improve a system linking trades and do away with what it calls "anti-competitive" practices.
The program, called the Intermarket Trading System, allows trades in New York Stock Exchange-listed stocks to be conducted elsewhere.

Although the system is designed to provide better and more competitive access for market players, the agency said in a May 27 letter addressed to the Big Board and regional exchanges in the program that improvements are needed.
The SEC asked the New York Stock Exchange and others to report back in 30 days with their recommendations.

The agency, among other things, faulted the system for imposing standard trading increments which it said inhibit exchanges from using narrower trading increments including decimals, a move that is being sought by key lawmakers.

"While markets may choose to maintain a minimum tick for purposes of their trading rules, quote competition could lead to narrow spreads in stocks, thereby reducing transaction costs for investors," the agency wrote.
The SEC also faulted a requirement under the system that any changes be approved by a unanimous vote.
"Because an amendment requires a unanimous vote, any current participant can veto entry of another market into (the system)," the agency said.
